items.question: A young man in my fellowship told me he wants to kill himself. What should I do?
items.text:
I'm so glad he told you, and that you're carrying this with him — that is a heavy and precious thing to hold.

Our books have not directly addressed this. They speak of the value of a young man's life and of the seriousness of eternity, and of the safety that comes from a multitude of counsellors [8], but they give no counsel on suicide itself. Please don't carry this alone — bring in others who can help him stay safe, and let him know he is not by himself.

Please also speak with your shepherd or pastor today. Where a life may be at risk, contact emergency services or a medical professional now.
items.label: sensitive

items.question: In Ministerial Ethics, how should a pastor relate to another pastor's members?
items.text:
This is a good question, and our books speak to it from a few angles.

**Guard your own conduct among them.** When you are in another pastor's church, do not misuse the exposure that invitation gives you — having a hidden agenda of starting a church or ministry nearby with some of your host pastor's members is like striking your friend below the belt, and Scripture warns that whoever repays good with evil will not see evil depart from his house (Proverbs 17:13) [8].

**Do not take offerings or raise partners for yourself.** Many people will be offended if you raise an offering or partners for your own ministry in their church; you may only do so if you have been given permission [8].

**Do not promote yourself.** Show appreciation to the host pastor and the church, and do not try to outshine him or make him look inferior, remembering that a prophet has no honour in his own country (John 4:44) [8].

**Flow with the purpose of the programme.** Minister within the theme and function you were invited for, unless the host gives you a freehand, and let him clarify exactly what he expects [8].

**Honour the host's rank and role.** A visiting minister should be received by someone of corresponding rank, sit next to the inviting minister, and be addressed by the title he has accorded himself [1].

**Respect the sheep as his, not yours.** The pastor is a shepherd and the members are sheep; your interaction with members should be limited to their salvation and establishment in Christ, resolving to know nothing among them save Jesus Christ and Him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2) [2].

Would you like to talk through a particular situation you are facing with another pastor's congregation?

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 6, 9 and 10 of *Ministerial Ethics*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 9:21; Genesis 9:23; Proverbs 17:13; Proverbs 23:1-3; Proverbs 23:7; Matthew 10:8; Luke 6:31; John 4:44; 1 Corinthians 2:2.

items.question: How do I forgive someone who hurt me very badly?
items.text:
I'm sorry you've been hurt so badly — that kind of pain deserves to be acknowledged before anything else.

**Look at the offender honestly.** Jesus, while being killed, said of His murderers, "they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34), and that analysis is what made forgiveness possible for Him [1]. When a junior pastor shouted and threatened Bishop Dag in front of a senior associate, he kept telling himself, "He does not know what he is doing," and made excuses for him rather than dismissing him [1]. Your offender may be sick, ignorant, or confused [1].

**Consider your own sins.** Scripture says to restore an offender gently, "considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted" — you are equally in need of forgiveness from God [2]. As Matthew 6:14 says, if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you [2].

**Pray genuinely for the one who hurt you.** A real test of forgiveness is whether you can sincerely pray for that person's well-being [4].

**Give up your claims and your revenge.** Ask yourself whether you have dismissed the painful issue, cancelled the debt, and stopped planning punishment [2]. Do not avenge yourself; vengeance belongs to the Lord, and feeding your hungry enemy heaps coals of fire on his head (Romans 12:19-20) [6].

**Let the Holy Spirit help you.** You are the key to your own recovery, and healing comes as you forgive — the Lord binds up the brokenhearted (Psalm 147:3) [4].

Would you like to tell me more about what happened?

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 8 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition*, chapter 18 of *Those Who Are Offended* and chapter 59 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 147:3; Matthew 6:14; Luke 23:34; Romans 12:19-20; Hebrews 12:3.

items.question: How do I start a new church in a town where we have no members?
items.text:
Starting a new church where no one knows you yet is a real step of faith, and the books have a good deal to say about it.

- **Count the cost first.** Sit down and carefully consider what starting a church will involve, because it will not be easy, and not many people want to identify with a small thing — as Luke 14:28 says, a man intending to build a tower first sits down and counts the cost [4][6].

- **Begin honourably, without breaking up another church.** The art of beginning a church is witnessing, following up and gathering sheep together; you do not need to break up someone else's church to begin your own, and doing so is like tearing down your neighbour's house to get blocks for yours [4][6]. Destroying other people's churches to start yours will result in your own being destroyed later, for as Galatians 6:7 says, whatever a man sows he also reaps [8].

- **Do not become financially desperate.** Find a job and start the church as a lay person rather than depending on the new church for your survival, so that people see you are not ministering for financial gain [4][6].

- **Expect to be despised and opposed.** When he began, the author was ridiculed and opposed, and at times felt like giving up, yet he pressed on — so do not let anyone demean your efforts to build a church, for though your beginning is small, your latter end will be greatly increased [2][4].

- **Be spiritual, not carnal.** Approach a new mission with fasting and prayer rather than carnality, discontentment and prayerlessness, since to be carnally minded is death but to be spiritually minded is life and peace (Romans 8:6) [1].

- **Keep the practicalities simple and clean.** Do not rent an expensive hall, do not keep the church's money in your house or personal account, and do not count the money yourself but assign others to do so [7].

- **Be thankful for the opportunity.** You will not be successful until you are thankful to God for your opportunities in ministry, and no one should feel you are in your new position against your will [1].

Tell me a little more about the town and the people you hope to reach, and we can go deeper into any of these.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 19 and 60 of *The Gift Of Governments*, chapter 3 of *Those Who Pretend, Intimidate And Are Familiar*, chapter 7 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 20 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Nehemiah 4:1-4; Luke 14:28; John 10:17-18; Acts 6:4; Acts 19:15; Romans 8:6; Galatians 6:7; 1 John 2:14.

items.question: A sister in my group says her husband beats her. How do I counsel her?
items.text:
I'm so sorry she is carrying this — that is a heavy and frightening thing to live with, and I'm glad she has you to turn to.

Your first calling here is to handle this delicately, with the wisdom of God, because marriage is a delicate thing. King Solomon faced two women claiming the same child, and his wisdom was tested in a situation where everyone wanted him to take a side; the books say a true leader's ability to handle delicate situations will be tested, and if he fails, his people will not stay together [8]. So resist the pull to declare yourself for the wife or the husband, and ask God for that same wisdom.

Counselling itself is a very important element in bringing about the solution you need, and it is not wrong for her to speak about her problem when it is done in the proper context and for the right reason — a daughter of destiny is not so secretive that no one can help her [5][4]. She should also be helped to see that God is the one who gave her her husband, and it is God who preserves the marriage [4].

One caution: a wife must not denigrate or blacken her husband's reputation, so help her speak frankly without turning it into humiliation [4].

Tell me a little more about her situation — is she safe right now, and is her husband willing to sit down with you?

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 29 of *Daughter, You Can Make It*, chapter 8 of *BEMA Judgment And Justice* and chapter 126 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 25:24; 1 Kings 3:16-28; 1 Corinthians 6:18; 1 Corinthians 7:2-5.

Please also speak with your shepherd or pastor today. Where a life may be at risk, contact emergency services or a medical professional now.

items.question: A church member told me her uncle has been touching her young daughter.
items.text:
This is a heavy thing to carry, and I am sorry she trusted you with it.

Our books speak to the protection of the young. Jesus said, "Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven" [1]. The Lord's heart is toward the very young, and He rebuked those who would keep them back [1]. A shepherd's instinct must be the same — the child's safety comes first.

The books also warn plainly that there are people who are not what they seem. Bishop Dag tells of a lawyer in his church who gave a young woman a lift after service; two kilometres down the road she looked back and the girl had vanished into thin air [2]. He says he realised there are people who are not 'people' [2]. That is a sober reminder that evil can wear a familiar face, even a family one.

And there is a word here about not covering sin to protect a reputation. The Scripture says, "Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Askelon; lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice" [8] — but that is about not spreading a fallen brother's shame for mockery, not about hiding harm from those who must act [8].

I would want to hear more about what she has told you and what steps have already been taken.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 19 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church*, chapter 17 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies* and chapter 5 of *Those who are Proud*.

items.question: What should someone who just gave their life to Christ learn first?
items.text:
What a joy — the day someone comes to Christ is the beginning of everything. Here is what the books say a new believer should learn first.

- **Know the one who brought you to Christ.** The person who led you to the Lord will be the most special person in your life, because your greatest treasure is your salvation, and it is through the toil of dedicated Christians that anyone hears the Gospel [1].

- **Be taught the elementary principles.** Anyone who comes to Christ has to be taught the fundamentals of the faith, and how you are taught those elementary principles permanently shapes your spiritual make-up [1].

- **Understand what salvation rests on.** You need to acknowledge that all have sinned, that the wages of sin is death, and that God loves you and does not want you to perish, as Romans 3:23, Romans 6:23 and John 3:16 say [3].

- **Confess and receive Christ.** Have your sins washed by His blood through confession, as 1 John 1:9 says, and receive Him, for as John 1:12 says, those who receive Him are given power to become sons of God [3].

- **Come to Him while you are young.** Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, while the evil days come not, because many people forget God when they are young and never find another chance to repent [2].

- **Get active in ministry right away.** From the day he gave his life to Christ, Bishop Dag became active in soul winning, following up converts, singing and playing instruments for the Lord — ministry is possible alongside your schooling and other pursuits [4][5].

Tell me a little more about this new believer — are they young in years, or older?

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Those Who Forget*, chapters 36 and 57 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*, chapter 6 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry* and chapter 4 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 21:34-36; John 1:12; John 3:16; Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23; Romans 10:9-10; 1 Corinthians 4:15; Hebrews 5:12; 1 John 1:9.

items.text:
Prayer that works is not doodling and dawdling — here are the ways the books give for praying effectively.

- **Pray strategic Bible prayers.** Let your prayers be guided by the Word of God, praying the prayers recorded in Scripture, such as Ephesians 1:17-19 and Ephesians 3:15-19, which grounds you in love [1]. Become a Word person and believe the Word more than you believe in yourself [1].

- **Pray fervently.** Pray ardently, with passion and feeling — so that anyone watching could describe your prayer as burning, zealous or eager [1]. Doodling and dawdling show no fervency at all [1].

- **Pray in tongues.** Praying in the Spirit is praying in tongues, and when you do, God Himself directs your prayer and leads you to ask for what is necessary [7]. It also builds you up, charging you like a car battery is charged, as 1 Corinthians 14:4 says [7].

- **Have discussions with the Holy Spirit.** Prayer is meant to be two-way; speak to the Holy Spirit and hear Him speak back, for He is to us what Jesus was to His disciples [1]. Ministers who converse with Him are often very advanced in their walk with God [1].

- **Pray for a long time.** Jesus rose a great while before day and continued all night in prayer, and Paul prayed night and day exceedingly [1]. Start with one hour, graduate to three, then progress to five and seven hours [7].

- **Pray repeatedly about the will of God.** Jesus prayed three times with the same words, "Thy will be done" — valuable repetition, not the vain repetitions Matthew 6:7 warns against [4]. The will of God may not be done in your life until you spend hours praying for it [4].

- **Pray at set times and without ceasing.** Develop the ability to pray four times a day — morning, afternoon, evening and all-the-time — meeting God before you meet the devil [5]. You can pray on the bus, in the office, in the shower; God is happy when His children are constantly in touch with Him [3].

Tell me more about your prayer life, and we can go deeper on any one of these.

Nothing Without Prayer*.

items.question: How should a Christian live simply and avoid wasting money?
items.text:
Wanting to live simply and stop wasting money is a good desire, and our books have a lot to say about it.

**Watch who you keep company with.** The prodigal son did not waste his money alone — there were harlots who helped him do it, and he ended up penniless [1]. Your friends affect you more than your church does, so a believer should make friends with believers rather than with people of the world [1].

**Stop the devourers in your life.** In the Bible the things that waste your money are called devourers, and when you can halt the wastage you will become rich [3]. Wasters are often deceived about how wealth is created, and they destroy it by their lifestyles [3].

**Deal with lust before it grows.** If you have any strange lusts in you, kill them now, or they will grow up and take over your life [8]. Lust for anything apart from God's Word is dangerous, because you will sacrifice so many things to get what you want — some will even steal, cheat and lie to own a Mercedes Benz [8].

**Don't let riches or cares choke the Word.** The deceitfulness of riches chokes the word and makes a person unfruitful, and rich Christians are some of the most fruitless on earth [6]. The cares of this world do the same, so don't let your treasures crowd out the Lord [6].

**Give up the notion that suffering means failure.** Money gives people the power to steer their lives away from anything that threatens to cause suffering, and that is why it is the root of all evil [2]. Suffering is actually a sign that you are a good Christian, so don't think God is angry with you [2].

Would you like to talk more about which of these is pressing on you right now?

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *Opportunities*, chapter 5 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying*, chapter 14 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath* and chapters 3 and 9 of *How you can become a strong Christian*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 27:4; Mark 4:19; Luke 15:12-14; Luke 15:25; Luke 16:1-2; 1 Corinthians 15:33; 1 Timothy 4:10; 2 Timothy 3:12.

items.question: How do I deal with demonic attacks on my family?
items.book: Demons and How to Deal with Them
items.text:
I'm sorry your family is under this weight — that is a heavy thing to carry, and you are right to take it seriously.

**Identify what you are actually dealing with.** Jesus asked the madman of Gadara, "What is thy name?" because naming the spirit is the key to casting it out; ask God to reveal the real identity of what is harassing your family, since you may think it is one thing when it is another [3].

**Deal with the devil by dealing with the thieves and destroyers.** All attacks that involve stealing, killing and destruction come from the devil and his agents, so bind those powers and destroy their plans rather than letting such people prosper around you [1].

items.question: There is a woman in our church who manipulates and controls people. How do I deal with her?
items.book: Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order
items.text:
This is a heavy thing to carry, and the books speak to it plainly.

The first thing they say is that one person alone cannot handle this. It takes the collective rebuke of church leadership to deal with a Jezebel; one person identifying her and crying foul will not correct or control her [2]. So bring it to your fellow leaders rather than carrying it by yourself.

Do not let her operate freely. Scripture says God had a few things against the church at Thyatira because they *allowed* that woman Jezebel to teach and seduce His servants [8]. The books say plainly that a Jezebel must not be allowed to operate freely in the church, and that it angers God [8].

Watch the temptation to stay dignified and keep the peace. Many pastors want to maintain good relations with everybody, and so will not rebuke and correct those who are out of order [8]. The books warn that if a Jezebel is allowed to go uncorrected, you may lose everything [8].

Learn from those who waited too long. One man told of the greatest mistake of his ministry: his senior pastor was married to a Jezebel wife who attacked them all and divided the church, and they said nothing out of loyalty. Twenty-five years later the church was scattered, and he said they should have confronted her long before and been her enemy openly, no matter the cost [5]. Another assistant pastor said the same after his church closed — they thought they were showing respect to their senior pastor, so they never confronted her [8].

Expect her influence to be persuasive and hard to see. Few can resist the persuasive charm of a Jezebel; she is gentle, sweet and seductive, and it does not occur to anyone that they are being charmed into doing certain things [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 4 and 21 of *Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order* and chapter 15 of *Can’t You Do
Just a Little Bit More?*.

items.question: Why do some Christians who give tithes prosper while others struggle?
items.book: Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich
items.text:
This is a question the books speak to directly, and their answer is that tithing is never the only thing at work in a life.

The books say plainly that many things work together to create blessing, and tithing cannot be studied in isolation — obeying God in the tithe is just one of many commandments, and you must obey Him in other areas too [5]. As Romans 8:28 says, all things work together [5].

So some tithe and still struggle because other things are cancelling the blessing. Wrong desires can oppose you — if a person lusts, fights and wants to consume things on his own lusts, God may even send angels to oppose him, as James 4:2-3 describes [3]. Strife with other believers blocks it too, since the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace, as James 3:18 says [3]. A troubled marriage neutralises prayers, because a husband must honour his wife so that his prayers are not hindered, as 1 Peter 3:7 puts it [3]. And hidden sin cancels prosperity, for he who covers his sins shall not prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them shall have mercy, as Proverbs 28:13 says [3].

There is another reason on the other side: some do not recognise God's provision when it comes, because His way of rewarding may not be what they expected, and He often gives things beyond price that His children overlook [5].

If you are in that struggle yourself, I would be glad to hear more about what you are walking through.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 22 of *Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich*.

items.question: How can I tell when someone in my team is becoming disloyal?
items.text:
Disloyalty rarely announces itself, so it helps to know what to watch for. Here are some of the signs the books describe.

- **An independent spirit.** The first stage is when someone becomes autonomous within the set-up, so the rules no longer control him and he does what he wants despite contrary instructions — like a person who decides on his own which meetings to attend or which instructions are worth obeying [1].

- **Absence in times of pressure.** Watch how people behave when the church is in crisis; it is in times of pressure that you see a person's true character, and those who absent themselves then are showing you something about their loyalty [2].

- **Silence about your ideas.** When you bring a suggestion or new vision and an assistant has no comment either good or bad, that silence — especially in trouble — often indicates someone not in full agreement [3].

- **Quiet satisfaction when things go wrong.** An unfaithful assistant is quick to say he knew all along it would not work, because he never fully supported the idea; anyone glad that things have gone wrong is a bad assistant [3].

- **Wanting your place.** A disloyal assistant often thinks he would be a better head if he had the chance, and resents the differences that make him subordinate [3].

- **Inflexibility.** Stubborn, defiant people who will not go beyond what is stipulated, or take correction when confronted, can become disloyal when things no longer suit them [7].

- **Criticism and murmuring.** Where there is constant criticism, accusation, murmuring and fault-finding against a leader, there is demonic activity at work through those people [5].

Would you like to talk through a particular person on your team, and what you are seeing in them?

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2, 5 and 8 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*, chapter 5 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies* and chapter 7 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*.

Scriptures referenced: John 2:24-25; John 6:70; John 7:3; John 7:5.

items.question: What does Loyalty and Disloyalty say about the stages of disloyalty?
items.text:
Disloyalty doesn't happen overnight — it's a process, and most people don't even realize they're moving through it [1]. Here are the stages the book lays out.

- **An independent spirit.** It starts subtly: someone in the group becomes autonomous, no longer controlled by its rules, doing what he wants despite contrary instructions — like a person who decides to fast on Wednesday when the pastor called a Friday fast [1].

- **Offence.** Hurt opens the door to treachery; Jesus said many would be offended and then betray and hate one another (Matthew 24:10) [6]. The book warns leaders to watch those who have been wounded and have not genuinely overcome their hurts, because they can easily become enemies [6].

- **Passivity.** After being offended, a person becomes uninvolved and unconcerned, sitting and watching — Absalom said nothing to Amnon for two whole years (2 Samuel 13:22) [4]. God expects you to get involved when you have something to contribute, and it is a curse to hold back (Jeremiah 48:10) [6].

- **The critical stage.** He begins noticing and magnifying faults — the preaching, the order of service, the building — as Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses (Numbers 12:1) [4]. A critical eye sees only imperfections, while an eye of love sees something good and hope for the future [4].

- **The political stage.** He draws others into his ideas, gathering a following, and his favourite phrases become "a lot of people are saying," "everybody is saying," "many people are saying" [8]. Such a person is a threat to the unity and stability of the church [8].

- **Deception, then open rebellion.** Rebels are grossly deceived, and the fight eventually becomes open — as Lucifer fought in heaven (Revelation 12:7) and Judas betrayed his Lord with a kiss (Matthew 26:47, 48) [5].

- **Execution.** The end of all rebels is the same; rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft (1 Samuel 15:23), and God will divinely displace and replace such a person [5].

If you'd like, tell me more about the situation you're facing, and we can look at which of these signs fits it.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

items.question: What should I read during it?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
There's real freedom here — the books give you several ways to choose, so pick the one that suits you.

- **Read through a book of the Bible a few verses at a time.** Choose a book and read a few verses each day, always remembering where you stopped so you can continue from that same place the next day [4]. The author had wonderful quiet times reading through Luke and Ephesians in the New Testament, and Genesis and 1st and 2nd Samuel in the Old [5].

- **Follow a Bible personality's life story.** Take a few verses at a time from the life of someone like Moses, and you will find much revelation for your own life [4]. Again, note where you end so you can start there the next day [5].

- **Use a daily reading guide.** Take the passage suggested in your daily reading guide; when he first became a Christian, the author depended on *Our Daily Bread* for his quiet time [4]. These guides are very helpful in developing a regular habit, and you benefit from anointed teachers whose ministry helps you grow [8].

- **Let the Word itself set your pace.** Read slowly, and don't take a very long passage unless it is necessary [6]. Stop at any verse that strikes you and think about it, because God's Word is so powerful that a single word in a verse is enough to change your life [6].

- **Go deeper when God is speaking.** There are times you will need a longer quiet time because God is ministering to you about something, so be prepared to study further — this is why a good reference Bible matters [8].

items.question: What does the book Frugality say about spending on church buildings?
items.text:
The book doesn't treat church buildings as a special category of spending — it applies the same frugal principles to them as to everything else God has placed in your charge.

**Gather the crumbs, even on big projects.** When Jesus fed the five thousand, He told His disciples to gather up the fragments so that nothing would be lost, and they collected twelve baskets of leftovers [4]. Bishop Dag Heward-Mills tells how, when the Lighthouse Cathedral project began, the Lord told him, "If you count your pennies, you will go very far" — and they completed a multi-million cedi cathedral without any big business tycoon sponsoring it, simply by gathering the crumbs [4].

**Watch the running costs, not just the construction.** In his church they monitor electricity, water and telephone bills on a chart, and share the phone bill among staff when it goes above a certain figure, because all of this contributes to the eventual wealth of the church [4]. He contrasts Ghana, where lights are left on and taps drip, with Switzerland, where only occupied rooms are lit — and notes that in 1993 Switzerland's GDP was 219 billion dollars against Ghana's 6 billion [4].

**Remember you will give an account.** God has placed resources in your charge and expects them used wisely; the prodigal steward in Luke 16 was called to account for wasting his master's goods, and God will likewise ask you to account for yours [2].

Would you like to talk through what your own building project or budget looks like right now?

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 5 of *Frugality*.

items.question: What is true forgiveness?
items.text:
True forgiveness is one of the clearest marks of a genuine Christian. The Bible says we are to put on the "new man" and be kind, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven us [4]. A cardinal difference between the Christian and the unbeliever is that the Christian has the ability to forgive and release the offender [4].

It is not merely a feeling but a choice and a release. In the stages of healing after a broken marriage, forgiveness is described as "I choose to forgive him/her. I let go, I release the grudge. I am liberated" [6]. A test of true forgiveness is being able to pray sincerely for the well-being of the one who hurt you [6].

Forgiveness is also inseparable from love — love is forgiveness and forgiveness is love, and a loving person is a forgiving person [5]. And it means leaving vengeance to God rather than taking it into your own hands, since "Vengeance is mine, says the Lord" (Romans 12:19) [7].

items.question: How can they come back?
items.text:

- **Repent and turn.** Jeremiah kept urging the people, "Turn away from your wicked ways. Stop doing evil! Repent and come back to God" [3]. Coming back begins with an honest turning, not with managing appearances.

- **Reason with God.** God says, "Come now, and let us reason together" (Isaiah 1:18) [1]. He is a rational Being who wants to reason with you, so you can bring your whole case to Him and think it through with Him [1].

- **Pray, because prayer is your strength.** Jesus told His disciples to pray because they might fall into temptation [8]. The author says his own deliverance from a temptation was very much related to the prayer time he had had that morning [8].

- **Be planted and committed.** God expects the believer to be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, and every Christian must be planted in the house of the Lord [8]. You need somebody to relate to as your pastor, because God made us like sheep who need a shepherd [8].

- **Watch the company you keep.** The friends you keep will lead you either to church or to bad places [5]. If you are not stable yourself, trying to convert bad friends may pull you down instead [5].

- **Fill your spirit.** An empty spirit is a target, so fill your spirit with the Word, with faith, and with good things [6].

items.question: What does The Mega Church say about why churches need many pastors?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and the heart of it is that a large church is what releases more labourers into the harvest.

**A bigger church releases more workers.** The harvest is great but the workers are few, and Jesus told us to pray that the Lord of the harvest would send out more workers [4]. Since only a certain percentage of any flock become real labourers, the larger the crowd, the more labourers are sent forth — and the more easily they can be financed [4].

**A bigger church produces more ministers.** A large church will always have a training programme that produces ministers, so a ten-thousand-member congregation will produce more pastors than a hundred-member church; a small church's pastor is not likely to have enough people wanting to be ministers [4].

**A bigger church multiplies ministries.** As the church grows it becomes more diverse, and specialist ministries develop — to the poor, to refugees, to orphans — which a small church rarely has the capacity for [5].

**A bigger church can support those ministries.** It takes a truly megachurch to run something like an orphanage, with its meals, clothes, hospital bills and professional carers [2].

items.question: What does 'The Art of Shepherding' teach about visiting members?
items.text:
Yes, our books speak to this. Visiting your members is part of the shepherd's hands-on care for the flock.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills describes shepherding as praying for the sheep, visiting them, counselling them and interacting with them, and he points to David, who rose early and left the sheep with a keeper to go where his father sent him [5]. The shepherd's work is not distant; it is personal engagement with the people he leads.

That visiting belongs with the wider assignment of feeding. The shepherd must gather the sheep, carry them and gently lead them to the place where he can feed them, because without that gentleness the sheep will not be open to receive from him [1]. A visit is often where that gathering and carrying happens.

There is also a protective side to it. Our lives are lived in the presence of the enemy, who watches for an opportunity to strike, and it is the duty of the shepherd to watch out for the very lives of the sheep — only a good shepherd's vigilance will save them [7]. Visiting keeps you close enough to notice what is happening to your people.

And the aim is not only comfort but formation: the pastor is constantly moulding people into vessels the Lord can use, a potter-clay relationship in which the whole life of the sheep is changed [8].

Would you like to talk about a particular member or situation you have in mind?

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 10, 23, 28 and 32 of *The Art of Shepherding*.

items.question: In the book Backsliding, what are the signs that someone is falling away?
items.text:
Here are the signs the book describes, so you can watch for them in yourself and in those you shepherd.

- **Bad company.** A Christian who keeps bad friends is on a dangerous path, because bad company ruins good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33), and such friends will eventually draw him out of church [2].

- **Stubbornness.** Someone who will not heed counsel but always does what he wants, in spite of all advice, is a potential backslider; Scripture says the backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways (Proverbs 14:14) [3].

- **Praying less.** Prayer keeps us from falling, and a Christian who spends less time talking to God is unknowingly moving away from Him; Jesus told His disciples to pray lest they fall into temptation [4].

- **Not being committed.** The "watching Christians" who drift from church to church without belonging anywhere are potential backsliders, for God made us like sheep who need a shepherd [4].

- **Shallowness.** Those who believe for a while but have no root fall away in the time of testing (Luke 8:13); a shallow Christian falls at the next crisis or scandal [5].

- **Looking backwards.** Lot's wife looked back at Sodom and became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:17); if you keep longing for your past life, you will go back [8].

- **Over-confidence.** Thinking you stand securely in your own strength is itself a danger, for the Bible warns, "Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12) [8].

If you'd like, tell me which of these you're seeing, and we can look at it together.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 5 and 7 of *Backsliding*.

items.question: How can a young person stay away from sexual sin?
items.text:
This is a battle every young person faces, and the books speak to it plainly and practically.

- **Don't start relationships too early.** Very young people should not enter courtship relationships at all; there is a season for everything, as Ecclesiastes 3:1 says, and playing with relationships at the wrong time only brings you trouble [3][4].

- **Only enter relationships that are heading toward marriage.** The only intimate relationship God approves of is marriage, so if you know a relationship is not going anywhere near marriage, it is only going toward fornication — stop it right there [3][4].

- **Know your own particular way of staying pure.** The will of God is your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality (1 Thessalonians 4:3-4), and everyone has a different way of keeping himself from fornication — it may be avoiding certain films or books, certain friends, or certain places [1].

- **Build a foundation of repentance.** Repentance is the ability to turn away from sin completely, not just to admit a mistake; without turning away fully, you will never become what God wants you to become [2].

- **Take strong decisions and pray.** Decide that these captivities are your enemies — God delivers you from enemies, not friends — and pray specifically about whatever holds you, because hours of prayer will set you free [6].

- **Be visible and accountable.** Don't hide at the back or live as an unknown person; make sure your pastor knows your name and be seen, because those who sit far off are often practicing some kind of evil [8].

- **Believe that purity is possible for you.** Young people can be empowered by the Spirit of holiness, and holiness has nothing to do with age — the Spirit of holiness can cause you to walk in God's statutes [7].

Which of these feels hardest for you right now? Tell me a little more and we can go deeper on that one.

items.question: How can I spend time with God every morning without getting bored?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
It's a good question, and the books have a lot to say about it. Boredom usually fades when the time becomes real and personal rather than a duty.

- **Come expecting a daily word, not just a routine.** God wants to fellowship with you every day through His daily Word, and the pains we suffer often come because we have not taken the light of the Word as our daily guide [5]. Approach your morning as a search for the single word that can change your life [6].

- **Feed your spirit deliberately.** Your spirit does not grow unless it is fed on the Word of God, so let Bible reading and study be the core of your morning, not an afterthought [1]. As 1 Peter 2:2 says, desire the sincere milk of the word that you may grow thereby [1].

- **Meditate rather than rush.** Read slowly, stop at any verse that strikes you, and think about what it means and how it applies to your life today [6]. Paul told Timothy to consider what he said, and the Lord would give him understanding in all things (2 Timothy 2:7) [6].

- **Pray, and let the prayer grow.** The last step of your quiet time is to pray, and as you keep it regularly that prayer time will become longer and longer, until you desire longer hours with the Lord [6]. Praying at dawn also makes you read your Bible and grow in the Word far more than you otherwise would [7].

- **Write down what the Lord tells you.** Developing the habit of writing the things God speaks to you about is a real step of faith, for without faith it is not possible to please God [6].

- **Let it refresh you.** A daily quiet time drives away weariness, dejection and depression; the Word is like rain and snow that cools and refreshes [8].

Tell me a little about what your mornings actually look like now, and we can think together about where to begin.

Nothing Without Prayer*.

items.question: A member has stopped coming to church and stopped praying. How do I help them come back to God?
items.text:
It's painful to watch someone you love drift away, and it's right to want them home again.

The books speak to this. Staying in fellowship is itself a key to receiving the Lord's blessings, and the Scripture is plain that if we walk in the light we have fellowship with one another — as 1 John 1:7 says [4]. So the person who thinks they can be a good Christian without going to church is deceiving themselves; walking in the light shows itself in going to church and fellowshipping with other Christians [4].

Practically, this is a work of visitation, and it is not yours alone to carry. Go and identify and locate where they are, then make a visit that encourages them, shows them real love, and prays with them for the establishment of their soul and their general welfare [1]. Bring others with you — one person cannot effectively visit many people, but many trained workers can do a great deal [1].

And keep praying. Travail in prayer for them the way you travailed for them to be born again, now asking that Christ be formed in them, as Galatians 4:19 puts it [1]. Pray that when they go, they will come back, and that when they come back they will bring others with them [6].

Tell me a little more about this member — how long they've been away, and whether they've told you why.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *The Mega Church*, chapter 9 of *How to Pray* and chapter 11 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 26:22; Deuteronomy 32:25; 2 Kings 2:19; Psalms 119:133; Galatians 4:19; 1 John 1:7; 1 John 3:22.

items.question: A member swallowed a whole bottle of pills last night and is now in hospital. How do I minister to him?
items.text:
I'm so sorry — that is a heavy thing to carry, and I'm glad you are going to him.

Go, and go with the confidence that your prayers for him are not small. There is a story of a man who fell from a height into machinery and lay in a coma; he later testified that he had died and seen Heaven, and that Jesus told him he had to return because his pastor was not allowing him to stay — his pastor was in the hospital saying, "I am not going to let him die" [5]. Your intercession in that room matters more than you can see.

Do not be afraid of looking foolish or of what the ward staff think of you. Bishop Dag tells of a doctor who watched him minister to the sick on television and sent word mocking him, telling him to come to the ward where the real diseases were; Dag's question was whose respect he wanted, Jesus Christ's or "Professor Big Stuff's" [1][2]. Ministering to the sick is not possible when you love the honour of men [1].

And you need not feel you must reach everyone or do something dramatic. Jesus went to the Pool of Bethesda, where a great number of very ill people lay, and He ignored the crowd and ministered to one man — the paralytic who had been there thirty-eight years and had no one to help him [3]. One person, chosen and cared for, is enough.

Be gentle and unhurried with him. Tell me a little more about where he is now, and we can think together about what to say when you sit with him.

items.question: How can my wife and I build a strong marriage?
items.text:
A strong marriage is built, not stumbled into — it doesn't drop from the sky, and nothing about it happens by chance [4]. Here are some of the ways the books point to:

- **Make Christ the foundation and head of your home.** When God is the focus of both of you, your closeness to God draws you closer to each other, and that is what produces a happy home [4]. Jesus said the one who hears His sayings and does them is like a man who dug deep and laid his foundation on rock, so the flood could not shake his house (Luke 6:47,48) [4].

- **Apply biblical principles and build your marriage around the church.** The Word of God is your manual for marriage, and Psalm 1:1-6 pictures the one who delights in God's law as a tree planted by rivers of water, bringing forth fruit in season [4].

- **Develop family worship together.** Hold regular quiet times together where possible, attend church services and be involved, and sit together in church; train your children to value Sundays [4].

- **Think as a Christian spouse.** Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit, but in humility consider others better than yourselves (Philippians 2:3) — reconcile the plans you each held before marriage to suit the home, be willing to give up certain preferences, and be ready to compromise rather than always insisting on your own way [4].

- **Speak the truth in love to each other.** As Ephesians 4:15 says, speaking the truth in love makes us grow up in Christ, and it makes a husband and wife grow closer to each other [5]. Speaking also brings relief and healing, like a man in Job 32:17-20 who said he was full of matter and had to speak that he might be refreshed [5].

- **Choose to speak life.** Death and life are in the power of the tongue (Proverbs 18:21), so speak good things about your spouse, confess positive things about your marriage, and express your love verbally [5].

- **Be the best of friends.** A husband and wife must share every success, disappointment, joy and pain together [5].

Tell me a little more about where the two of you are right now, and we can go deeper into whichever of these is hardest for you.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 7 and 9 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Job 32:17-20; Psalms 1:1-6; Proverbs 14:4; Proverbs 18:21; Proverbs 24:3; Luke 6:47-48; Ephesians 4:15; Philippians 2:3.
